claims.text: Hold the dumbbells with a closed, palms-forward (supinated) grip, thumbs wrapped round the handles, arms hanging at the sides.

quotes.text: Grasp two dumbbells with a closed, supinated grip (palms facing forward and thumbs wrapped around the handles) and let your arms hang to your sides, close to your body, with your palms facing forward.
Hold a pair of dumbbells in an underhand (supinated) grip, arms hanging by your sides.

claims.text: Stand with the feet about shoulder-width apart and the knees slightly bent.

quotes.text: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, maintaining a slight bend in your knees.

claims.text: The elbows stay close to the body for the whole set and never travel back; letting them move slightly forward at the top is fine.

quotes.text: Keep your elbows close to your body throughout the exercise.
Don’t let your upper arms travel back during the curl. Keep them at your sides, or move them slightly forward.
Curl the dumbbells higher by allowing the elbows to move forward as the dumbbell reaches your chest

claims.text: Elbows moving forward while lifting put extra load on the front delts, and elbows moving back let you cheat the weight up; only a slight forward move at the top is fine (c3).

quotes.text: If your elbows move forward while you’re lifting the weight, it will put an additional load on your front delts, instead of focusing on your biceps. If your elbows move backward, you’ll also move the load from your biceps and be able to “cheat up” the weight.

claims.text: Swinging the body to use momentum is the sign of a weight that is too heavy; the fix is less weight and a controlled lift.

quotes.text: By adding more weight than you can lift, you might start to swing your body and use momentum to get the weight up.
quotes.where: Common mistakes, using too heavy weights

quotes.text: If you start to swing, you should probably remove some weight instead and focus on performing the movement with control.
Trunk movements together with knee flexions were visually monitored by the researchers to avoid possible cheating.

claims.text: Keep the wrists straight (neither bent up nor down) through the lift; bent wrists put extra load on them and can cause discomfort.

quotes.text: Maintain a neutral wrist position (avoid flexion and extension of your wrists)
Keep your wrists straight during the movement. If they’re bent, it can put an unnecessary load on them and lead to discomfort and maybe even injuries.
quotes.where: Common mistakes, not locking your wrists

claims.text: Because elbow structure differs between people, the dumbbells may hang slightly away from the sides; pick the hand position that keeps the wrist straight.

quotes.text: The dumbbell position selected should be one that is most comfortable for you and keeps the wrists aligned straight with the forearm.
As some of us show structural differences at the elbow, we may not be able to hold the dumbbells against our sides in the lowered position unless we force a bend at our wrists.

claims.text: Stand with the chest up and the shoulders set down and slightly back; do not shrug during the lift.

quotes.text: Stand with your chest up and shoulders slightly retracted and depressed.
avoid shrugging your shoulders during the lift keeping your scapulae (shoulders) depressed and retracted.

claims.text: Tempo (up = lifting phase, down = lowering phase): lift in about 1 s and lower slowly in about 2 s. A study protocol used 3 s per full repetition; ACSM advises moderate speed (1-2 s up, 1-2 s down).

quotes.text: The metronome was set so that each repetition duration was 3 s.
at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
Inhale and gently lower the dumbbells back towards your starting position.

claims.text: Breathe out as the dumbbells rise and in as they lower.

quotes.text: Exhale and slowly bend each elbow in unison

claims.text: The biceps is the main muscle worked (an EMG study found at least 50% of maximum biceps activity in dumbbell curls); the brachioradialis, a forearm muscle, also flexes the elbow, and StrengthLog lists the forearm flexors as secondary.

quotes.text: Although all protocols elicited a considerable level of activation of the biceps brachii muscle (at least 50% of maximum RMS), the contribution of this muscle for elbow flexion/extension varied among exercises.
Biceps brachii is a robust forearm supinator and an elbow flexor while brachioradialis, the most superficial muscle of the forearm considering the radial part, acts as an elbow flexor
The dumbbell curl primarily targets your biceps and brachialis (which lie beneath the biceps), but the forearm flexors are also involved as a secondary muscle group.

claims.text: The standing dumbbell curl loads the biceps across the whole elbow range, so a full range (arms straight at the bottom) is worthwhile.

quotes.text: The Incline Dumbbell Curl and the Dumbbell Biceps Curl resulted in a considerable neuromuscular effort throughout the whole elbow range of motion.

claims.text: The upper arms must not travel back during the curl; staying at the sides or moving slightly forward at the top is acceptable.

quotes.text: Don’t let your upper arms travel back during the curl. Keep them at your sides, or move them slightly forward.

claims.text: The body stays still and only the arms move.

quotes.text: Make sure to keep your elbows close to the body the entire time. Your body shouldn’t move, just the arms.

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Across all weight training (not curls specifically), the most common way people are hurt badly enough for an emergency department is a weight dropping on them, mostly with free weights.

quotes.text: The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%). A large number of injuries occurred with free weights (90.4%).

plate.viewWhy: Elbow bending happens front-to-back, so the elbow angle, elbow drift (c4, c13) and body swing (c5) all read side-on. Census view is side.
plate.equipment: One dumbbell per hand, standing on the floor line. No bench.
plate.start: Standing tall, feet shoulder-width, knees slightly bent (c2); arms hanging straight at the sides, palms forward, elbows close to the body (c1, c3); wrists straight (c6); chest up, shoulders down (c8).
plate.end: Elbows fully bent, dumbbells near the front of the shoulders (c3); upper arms still at the sides or slightly forward, never back (c13); wrists straight (c6); body in the same upright position as the start (c14).

checkpoints.label: Elbows at sides
checkpoints.what: Upper arms stay by the body and never travel back; slightly forward at the top is fine.

checkpoints.label: Straight wrists
checkpoints.what: Hand in line with the forearm, not bent up or down.

checkpoints.label: Still body
checkpoints.what: Torso and knees don't move; only the forearms travel.

mistake.what: Swinging: leaning back and driving with the hips and knees to throw the dumbbells up.
mistake.why: It happens when the weight is heavier than the arms can lift, and it takes work away from the biceps.

tells.text: Upper arms stay by your sides

grip.type: Closed, palms forward (supinated), one dumbbell per hand.
grip.width: Arms hanging at the sides, dumbbells close to the body; they may sit slightly out from the sides if that keeps the wrist straight (c7).
grip.wrist: Straight, in line with the forearm, for the whole lift.

setup.step: Pick a weight you can curl without swinging.
Stand with feet shoulder-width, knees slightly bent.
Take a closed, palms-forward grip, thumbs round the handles, arms hanging at your sides.
Chest up, shoulders down and slightly back.

posture.point: Elbows stay close to the body.
Upper arms never travel back; slightly forward at the top is fine.
Body stays still; only the arms move.
Lower until the arms are straight again (full range).

handlingMistakes.mistake: Swinging the body to get the weight up.
handlingMistakes.fix: Use a lighter dumbbell and lift with control.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Elbows drifting back, or forward before the top.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep the elbows at your sides; never let them travel back.
Keep the hand in line with the forearm; pick the dumbbell position that allows it.

rows.where: Front of the upper arm, through the whole lift
rows.means: The biceps are doing the work.
Usually means the elbows are moving forward.
rows.fix: Keep the elbows at your sides.

rows.means: Usually means the wrist is bending.
rows.fix: Straighten the wrist; go lighter if you can't.

risks.risk: Bent wrists under load can cause wrist discomfort.
Dropped weights, mostly free weights, are the most common way weight trainers get badly hurt.

zooms.right: Closed palms-forward grip, thumb wrapped, hand in line with the forearm.
zooms.wrong: Wrist bent back or curled toward the forearm.

zooms.right: Upper arm by the side at the top of the curl.
zooms.wrong: Elbow swung back behind the body to cheat the weight up.

libraryDiff.why: biceps as primary (c11: biceps activation, Oliveira 2009) and forearms as secondary (c11: brachioradialis, Marcolin 2018; StrengthLog 'forearm flexors') both match exercises.json. StrengthLog also names brachialis, which is text-only.
